title: Can You Roll Your Tongue?
sources: Sturtevant (1940, PNAS) reported tongue rolling in about 65% of people and proposed it was a simple dominant single-gene trait; later surveys give roughly 65–81%

Identical twins are often discordant for tongue rolling (Matlock 1952, J Heredity; Reedy et al. 1971; Martin 1975, Nature), so it is not a simple one-gene trait; Sturtevant later called it 'embarrassing' that it was still taught as Mendelian (Sturtevant 1965)
The ability can change with age and some people report learning it (Komai 1951; McDonald, 'Myths of Human Genetics', University of Delaware, 2011)

lines.text: Try to roll your tongue into a tube. Can you?
lines.caps: Try to *roll | your *tongue | into a *tube | Can you?

lines.text: About two out of three people can.
For decades, schools taught it came from one single gene.
lines.caps: For *decades | schools taught | it came from | *one single gene

lines.text: But here's the twist. That's a myth.
Identical twins have the same DNA, and one can roll while the other can't.
lines.caps: Identical *twins | have the *same DNA | and one *can | while the other *can't

lines.text: Some people even learn it with practice.
So, can you roll yours? Tell me below.
